abstract: 1. Reintroduced insect populations founded by few individuals can change in phenotype through founder effects, genetic drift and new environmental conditions. Butterfly wing spot patterns, their fluctuating asymmetry and their variability can reflect such changes and population stress. 2. We studied the spot pattern of the hindwing underside of 267 Phengaris teleius butterflies from the Polish source metapopulation at the time of their reintroduction to the Netherlands in 1990, and from the current Polish and Dutch metapopulations (2019-2020). We analysed the presence, size, asymmetry and fusion of the spots, and the shape and variability of the spot pattern. 3. The reintroduced Dutch metapopulation differed in spot pattern shape from both Polish ones and was less variable than the source metapopulation. The two Polish metapopulations did not differ from each other in shape. Dutch butterflies also had a more frequent spot 11 than the current Polish metapopulation and a larger spot 1 than the source ones, and the concordance between both wings in the presence of the facultative spots differed among metapopulations, being lowest in the Dutch one. Only the presence of spot 10 in females and spot fusion in males changed in the Polish metapopulation between 1990 and 2019. 4. These results agree with the founder effect and the loss of genetic variability after the reintroduction, although local adaptation or plasticity cannot be ruled out. Although based on a single reintroduction, these results suggest that spot pattern variability, measured from photographs, could complement the genetic monitoring of reintroduced insect populations.
